lesson.title: Applied Optimization: A Five-Step Method You Can Trust on Any New Problem
lesson.summary: Consolidate the optimization workflow into five explicit steps, then apply the full method start to finish on a fresh problem, a three-sided fence built against the side of a house.
lesson.body:
Every optimization problem worked through so far, the open box, the divided fence, the minimum-material can, the closest point on a parabola, maximum profit, has followed the exact same skeleton underneath its different surface details. It is worth naming that skeleton explicitly, because recognizing the pattern is what lets you walk into a brand new problem with confidence instead of starting from scratch each time.

The five steps are these. First, identify and name the quantities that are free to change, and assign them variable names. Second, write the objective function, the single quantity you are trying to maximize or minimize, in terms of those variables. Third, write the constraint equation that ties the variables together, the fixed resource or fixed requirement in the problem, and use it to eliminate all but one variable from the objective function. Fourth, before touching a derivative, determine the practical domain the remaining variable is allowed to range over, based on the physical meaning of the problem, not just the algebra. Fifth, find the critical points of the reduced objective function, verify each one with the first or second derivative test, and compare the result against the domain's endpoints (the Candidates Test) before declaring a final answer.

To see the full method run start to finish on something new, consider a gardener with 600 feet of fencing who wants to enclose a rectangular garden using the side of a house as one border, so fencing is only needed on the other three sides. Step one: let x be the length of each of the two sides perpendicular to the house, and let y be the length of the side parallel to the house, opposite it. Step two: the objective is area, A = xy. Step three: the constraint is 2x + y = 600, since two sides of length x and one side of length y use up all the fencing; solving for y gives y = 600 - 2x, and substituting produces A(x) = x(600 - 2x) = 600x - 2x^2.

Step four: the practical domain is 0 < x < 300, since y = 600 - 2x must stay positive. Step five: differentiate, A'(x) = 600 - 4x, and set it to zero to get x = 150. Confirm with the second derivative: A''(x) = -4, negative everywhere, so x = 150 is the global maximum on the domain. With x = 150, y = 600 - 300 = 300, and the maximum area is A = 150 * 300 = 45,000 square feet. As a final check, the objective approaches 0 as x approaches either 0 or 300, so the interior critical point at x = 150 is clearly the winner over any boundary behavior.

Every worked example in this unit fits inside these same five steps, only the objective function, the constraint, and the resulting domain change from problem to problem. The remaining chapters in this unit zoom in on step five specifically, the verification step, because that is the step most often shortchanged, and it is the step where a wrong answer is most likely to slip through unnoticed.
